What’s the best thing about dining on your own? The people-watching In this month’s food column, Jay Rayner wrote that: “The pleasures of eating alone are obvious. You get to eat what you want, how you want. It is one of adulthood’s great indulgences. But who admits to its other profound pleasure, the licence it gives you to spy on people?” You responded with some of your own experiences. ‘I’ve met some interesting people that way’ ‘Good eating for me is inextricably linked with good company’ ‘I take a good book and do some people-watching’ What being a care worker taught me: the human spirit needs more than the basics Community care worker, Sarah Beauclerk wrote about her moving experiences as a care worker which prompted readers to talk about what they learned looking after others. ‘This job taught me some things about our society that I strongly criticise and hate’ ‘Daily living aids and assistive technology can help people continue to live their lives with dignity’ Why the nights are getting brighter - but not in a good way Many of you who like to look up at the stars were concerned to hear satellite observations show light pollution is spreading and affecting the level of darkness across the world. ------- Please generate a story based on the sentences provided. Include keywords ['date', 'nose', 'significance', 'stomach', 'writing'] in the response. On a cold autumn date, Mara sat alone by the window of a small restaurant, a notebook open beside her plate. She had come with the simple intention of feeding her stomach, but as the candles flickered against the glass, she found herself doing what solitary diners have always done: watching.

A man at the bar kept rubbing the bridge of his nose as if trying to hold himself together. Two students in the corner laughed over cheap pasta. An elderly woman ate slowly, carefully, with the concentration of someone honoring the meal rather than merely finishing it. Mara, who made a habit of writing down fragments of strangers’ lives, wondered what private burdens and joys had brought each of them there.

Earlier that day she had finished a long shift as a care worker. She had helped Mr Hargreaves from his bed to his chair, listened to Mrs Patel repeat the same memory three times, and watched a frail retired teacher smile with relief when a simple mobility aid allowed him to pour his own tea. The work had taught her that dignity often lived in small details. A brushed coat. A clean spoon. A person being asked what they wanted rather than being told. The significance of those details stayed with her more than the exhaustion.

When she left the restaurant, the town looked strangely bright. The sky above was bruised with artificial glow, and only the boldest stars survived it. Mara remembered being a child and seeing constellations so sharp they felt close enough to touch. Now the night seemed edited, thinned out by streetlamps, billboards, and distant industrial light.

She stopped under that pale sky and opened her notebook again. She wrote that eating alone was never truly lonely if one paid attention. She wrote that care work revealed both the cruelty and kindness of society. She wrote that darkness itself was becoming something people would soon have to protect.

Then she closed the notebook and walked home, carrying with her the restaurant’s warmth, the day’s fatigue, and the uneasy beauty of a brightening night.
